newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Landing fees put question mark on Cathay.
newsitem.headline: Landing fees put question mark on Cathay.

text.p: Cathay Pacific Airways Ltd's growth prospects look good if Hong Kong's new airport, to be opened next year, does not price its fees out of the regional market, analysts said on Thursday.
"There is no doubt that airport operations and efficiencies are going to increase and there will be some firmness in yields," said Viktor Shvets, regional airline analyst at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.

But until airport authorities and airlines reach a compromise on landing fees at Chek Lap Kok, the site of the new airport, the long-term earnings outlook for the Hong Kong carrier is poor, Shvets said.
Cathay has also said it had cautious hopes about the airport due to open in April 1998.
"We are very excited about the new airport at Chek Lap Kok, provided it remains competitive," managing director David Turnbull said on Wednesday following the release of the firm's 1996 results.
The company reported net profit of HK$3.81 billion ($488 million) in 1996, up 27.9 percent over the previous year. The total was boosted by an exceptional gain of HK$541 million.

But analysts' earnings forecasts were cautious. Their projections assumed a positive impact from a slight decline in fuel prices and improved passenger yields flowing from a stronger yen, in their earnings models for the next three years.

Japan provides a large portion of Cathay's income. Passenger yields in 1996 fell a weaker-than-expected 5.7 percent, hurt by the yen's drop against the U.S. dollar over the year. However, expected large increases in landing and parking charges at Chek Lap Kok would have a major impact on earnings, analysts said.
Deutsche Morgan Grenfell's Shvets expected earnings to hit HK$4.0 billion in 1997 and HK$4.52 billion in 1998. But for 1999, he forecast a slowing in earnings growth to a profit of HK$4.67 billion.

"What I am assuming is that landing and parking fees will double in the last quarter of 1998," said Shvets. "That is less than what the government is suggesting, which is tripling or quadrupling them."
ING Barings regional airline analyst Mark Simpson saw the landing charge rising by only 50 percent in 1998.
"We are forecasting 12 percent (earnings) growth in 1997, excluding exceptional gains in 1996, 13 percent in 1998 and 17 percent in 1999," said Simpson.

The International Air Transport Association (IATA) has estimated a fully loaded jumbo jet would have to pay US$12,000 every time it landed at Chek Lap Kok. Analysts said the charge at the current Kai Tak airport is about US$4,000.

The Airport Authority, in charge of overseeing the building and future operation of the new airport, has said it was too early to speculate what the fees may be. Authority and IATA officials were meeting on Thursday to discuss the fees.
Shvets said landing fees at most airports in Southeast Asia are between US$2,000 and US$4,000, putting Hong Kong's US$4,000 already at the high end of the range.
On the other hand Tokyo's Narita airport charges more than US$11,000 and Osaka's new airport about US$10,000, he said.
"We are assuming that the airlines will have to cope with most of that increase without passing it onto consumers," said Shvets. "Competition will not allow them."
But there was no doubt Cathay could develop lucrative North American routes, allowing it to achieve some earnings growth in 1999, said Shvets.
Cathay executives were cautiously upbeat on the airline's growth prospects after the move to the new airport, which will provide greater capacity and operating efficiencies.

"We do have equipment coming in 1998 and we do have plans to mount a considerable number of increased services...increasing frequency on existing routes within Southeast Asia, said Cathay Pacific chairman Peter Sutch.
